member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Mongo.NoSql.Console.MongoConsoleGuard
member.summary:
Validates everything a query console accepts before any of it becomes a MongoDB command.
A console is, by design, someone typing queries at a database, so the guard's job is not to decide who may do that (the app does, with authorisation) but to keep what they type inside "query the data": no server-side JavaScript ($where, $function, $accumulator), no stage that writes a collection out ($out, $merge), no reaching outside the database through its name, and no update that isn't an explicit field operator.
Everything here is pure — parse and inspect only — so it is fully unit testable without a server.

member.name: F:KeshavSingh.Mongo.NoSql.Console.MongoConsoleGuard.AllowedUpdateOperators

member.name: M:KeshavSingh.Mongo.NoSql.Console.MongoConsoleGuard.RejectRedactedFieldReferences(MongoDB.Bson.BsonValue,KeshavSingh.Mongo.NoSql.Console.MongoConsoleOptions)
member.summary:
Refuses a pipeline that reads a secret field, whatever it calls the result.
Output-name redaction alone is not enough: {"$project": {"x": "$PasswordHash"}} emits the hash under a name no redaction list knows about. Since a pipeline can rename freely, the only reliable place to stop it is the field REFERENCE — a "$Field" string anywhere in the pipeline — so that is what this rejects.

member.name: T:KeshavSingh.Mongo.NoSql.Console.MongoQueryConsole
member.summary:
A guarded "query editor" over a MongoDB database — the SQL-console equivalent for apps that keep their data in Mongo. Every request goes through first, every read is bounded by a page size and a server-side time budget, every write is off unless the app turns it on, and configured secret fields are redacted on the way out.
This deliberately knows nothing about who is asking. Deciding that is the app's job: put this behind an admin-only endpoint, and log what gets run.
